# Comparative Analysis of Global Education Systems
Global education frameworks vary significantly in governance, funding, and structural rigidity. Russia maintains a state-controlled model with compulsory education extended to 11 years, while Pakistan struggles with chronic underfunding and regional disparities. In contrast, the Netherlands utilizes annual teacher assessments for progression, and Canada operates a decentralized system where provincial variations dictate curriculum and funding. Other nations, such as Mexico, operate highly stratified centralized systems facing corruption and low indigenous enrollment, whereas Bangladesh faces severe resource constraints leading to high teacher absenteeism. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has rapidly modernized its system since 1926, investing heavily in STEM and humanities, though it still struggles with inclusivity for students with severe disabilities.
Societal challenges range from intense academic pressure to deep-seated inequities. South Korea and Japan grapple with "shadow education" and mental health issues, while New Zealand confronts significant disparities between Māori and Pākehā students, along with widespread bullying and declining foundational math skills. Experts across these diverse contexts advocate for insulating education from political interference, reforming assessment methods to prioritize student welfare, and mastering basic skills before advancing to complex problem-solving to better align education with future economic demands.
